Sociologists use the term concentrated disadvantage to describe neighborhoods with overlapping poverty, joblessness, and family disruption. Whether such contexts shape life chances, or merely assemble people whose trajectories were already fixed, has structured the field's methodological quarrels for a generation. Christopher Jencks and Susan Mayer's 1990 review argued that existing neighborhood studies could not separate contextual influence from residential sorting. [1] Robert Sampson's book Great American City documented the persistence of neighborhood inequality in Chicago across several decades.

That unresolved impasse over separating context from sorting led directly to the adoption of within-family comparison as a remedy. Sibling-difference designs hold constant characteristics shared by children of the same parents. The selection problem arises when unmeasured characteristics of residents determine which neighborhoods they live in.

It was precisely because the determinants of residential location remain unmeasured that the discipline turned toward designs resting on chance assignment. Unlike strategies that hold fixed whatever children of the same parents have in common, this newer approach seeks its leverage in variation imposed from outside the household. Randomized housing mobility experiments are designed to break the link between family characteristics and neighborhood context, and that design logic led researchers to use housing voucher lotteries as instrumental variables to identify neighborhood effects. That ambition to sever family background from neighborhood context resulted in the Moving to Opportunity demonstration, launched by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development in 1994.

Moving to Opportunity assigned participating families to its treatment and control groups by lottery, which shows that voucher allocation can indeed serve as the identifying instrument in work of this kind. Random assignment of that sort and purely observational inference are mutually exclusive: either the demonstration allocated units by lottery, or it relied entirely on observational comparisons of volunteer families with no random assignment, and exactly one of those two descriptions can hold of it. The demonstration enrolled roughly 40,000 families across twenty American cities. Its age gradients repay close attention. Children in Moving to Opportunity families who relocated after age eighteen showed the largest adult earnings gains, a pattern that stands in sharp contrast to what the interim evaluation reported about adult labor-market outcomes.

Those interim results became available only after the 1994 launch of the demonstration. The interim Moving to Opportunity evaluation documented improvements in adult mental health among movers. The same interim evaluation detected no significant effects on adult employment or earnings. [2] Adjudication between contextual and individual accounts therefore rests less on any single finding than on whether a design can credibly claim that neighborhood exposure was fixed by something other than the residents themselves.

Adjudicating between the claim that ego depletion was never real and the claim that the failed replications simply departed from the original procedure requires separating questions of evidential strength from questions of procedural fidelity. Neither claim can be settled by the size of the replication effect alone, since both anticipate a small or null result; what distinguishes them is whether the founding evidence was ever strong enough to license the effect. The original 1998 ego depletion experiments used samples of roughly 60 participants each. [1] The original 1998 experiments each enrolled more than 2,000 participants, a figure that cannot be squared with the sample sizes just described, since one and the same set of studies cannot have been run at both scales. [2]

After that 2014 analysis appeared, Hagger and colleagues coordinated a Registered Replication Report on ego depletion, published in 2016. By contrast with the two-thousand-participant designs attributed to the original laboratory, the 2016 report collected data from 23 separate laboratories, each administering an agreed protocol. Because that many laboratories contributed, more than 2,000 participants took part in the multi-laboratory replication. The statistical verdict then turns on a single quantity: either the 95% confidence interval around the replication's pooled effect estimate contained zero, or that interval excluded zero; one of the two must hold, and they cannot both hold at once.

Interpretation of the outcome divides along two lines, and at least one of them is correct, perhaps both: publication bias inflated the effect sizes reported in the original ego depletion literature, and the letter-crossing task used in the replication did not deplete participants' self-control. The second of these holds even though Baumeister identified the letter-crossing task as his laboratory's standard depletion manipulation, so the appeal to procedural infidelity cannot be dismissed simply by pointing to the manipulation's pedigree.

Precisely because that manipulation failed to deplete self-control, methodologists have pressed for a procedural remedy that forecloses after-the-fact disputes about fidelity. Adversarial collaboration brings original and replicating researchers together to agree on a protocol in advance, and it was this arrangement that led to the replication protocol being circulated to the original authors before data collection began. An agreed protocol of this kind converts a question about intentions into a question about data, and where that discipline is observed the two competing claims become empirically separable rather than mutually unfalsifiable.

[1] The distinction carries weight because fatigue surfaces point to a service history of repeated loading, while a clean overload surface points to a member that was never adequate for the demand placed upon it.

Material quality is measured rather than inferred from the appearance of the rubble. Concrete cores extracted from the wreckage are tested for compressive strength. Concrete compressive strength is determined by measuring the electrical resistivity of core samples, a method of determination that cannot be squared with the crushing of extracted cores to destruction in a press. Finite element models are built to reconstruct the load paths that existed in the structure before failure. That modelling shows that the calculated capacity of the failed connection was lower than the load demand imposed on it; in other words, the load demand on the failed connection exceeded its computed strength.

The loading condition at the instant of failure is fixed from toll records, dashboard-camera footage and the accounts of witnesses on the approaches. Exactly one of two states obtained: the bridge was carrying traffic at the moment of the collapse, or the bridge was closed to all traffic at the moment of the collapse, one of these being necessarily the case and the two being mutually exclusive. Whichever of them held governs the live load that any numerical reconstruction of the failure must reproduce.

Once the technical record is assembled, the accounts offered by the parties diverge sharply. The design engineer attributed the collapse to the contractor's departure from the specified post-tensioning sequence, whereas the contractor attributed the collapse to an under-designed truss connection node. After the design engineer had advanced that attribution, a statutory public inquiry was constituted, and such an inquiry has the power to compel witnesses to give evidence under oath. Subsequently, the commission of inquiry held that the primary cause of the collapse was a deficiency in the original design. Even though the coercive authority of such a body reaches no further than obliging witnesses to testify on oath, the findings of fact made by an official inquiry are binding on criminal courts in every jurisdiction.

Disputes of this kind are settled in practice by a layered procedure in which the trained eye, the archive and the instrument are brought to bear in turn. Connoisseurship comes first and carries real weight, since it rests on long comparative acquaintance with a master's handling of light, contour and impasto. Abraham Bredius authenticated "The Supper at Emmaus" as a work by Johannes Vermeer, and that verdict from the most authoritative connoisseur of the day led the Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen in Rotterdam to purchase the painting.

The documentary and the physical approaches answer different questions and must not be conflated. Provenance research traces the documented ownership history of a painting, whereas radiocarbon dating establishes the year of a painting's execution to within a single year. Neither procedure is self-sufficient, for a chain of ownership can be fabricated by an obliging dealer and a physical measurement can be misread by an incautious analyst.

When the archive falls silent, the question passes to the laboratory bench, where the substance of the object is interrogated directly. Paul Coremans led the laboratory examination of the disputed Vermeers. Phenol-formaldehyde resin, a wholly synthetic medium, was identified in the paint layers of the disputed pictures. [1] Van Meegeren, by then a figure of considerable public notoriety, stood trial in Amsterdam in 1947. The trial resulted in a sentence of one year in prison.

The probative force of such findings lies wholly in the chronology of artists' materials. Phenol-formaldehyde resin was first manufactured in the twentieth century; synthetic ultramarine, by contrast, became commercially available in the seventeenth century. The twentieth-century date at which the resin entered manufacture shows that the paint layers of the disputed picture contain a material unavailable to seventeenth-century painters. [2] At least one of two marks of fabrication is accordingly present in the picture — a substance beyond the reach of any seventeenth-century studio in its paint film, or a craquelure artificially induced across its surface — and perhaps both are.

The presence of an anachronistic material in the paint film cannot be squared with the proposition that "The Supper at Emmaus" was executed during Vermeer's lifetime. Either the picture was executed during Vermeer's lifetime or it was executed after Vermeer's death; one of these must be the case and they cannot both be, and no refinement of stylistic sympathy can make the paint film older than the chemistry that produced it. That is why, when connoisseurial conviction and laboratory findings point in opposite directions, the material evidence is given the last word: a judgment of quality can be revised, but a pigment cannot be made to exist before it was invented.

Disputes of this kind are seldom resolved by declaring one explanation right and the other wrong; they are resolved by asking which account better predicts the surviving distribution of evidence. The oldest systematic answer still frames the debate: Edward Gibbon attributed Christianity's success to five secondary causes. Any serious reconstruction must concede at least one of two things, and perhaps both: that the movement's distinctive doctrines contributed to its rapid early growth, or that the social conditions of the surrounding society contributed to that growth. That the surrounding conditions did part of the work is indicated by E. R. Dodds's characterization of the third-century Roman world as an age of anxiety, a diagnosis of collective insecurity for which the religious market supplied remedies.

Where Gibbon proceeded by enumerating five secondary causes, the sociological turn in the study of Christian expansion has run in the opposite direction, beginning from the mechanisms by which recruits are actually recruited rather than from a catalogue of causes. Lofland and Stark's 1965 study of a new religious movement found that converts joined through pre-existing interpersonal ties, and that finding led Stark to apply sociological models of modern conversion to the early Christian movement. That transfer of models yielded a quantitative result: Stark posited that Christianity grew at about 40 percent per decade. He also estimated growth at roughly 70 percent per decade, and the two figures cannot both be correct, so the arithmetic of the curve is itself part of what scholars must adjudicate before they can weigh doctrine against environment.

Demographic shocks occupy a central place in the social-conditions case, since mortality crises test a community's capacity for care and burial. [1] The documentary record can be dated on its own terms: Pliny the Younger wrote to the emperor Trajan about Christians in Bithynia around 112 CE, decades before the Antonine Plague, and more than a century before the house church at Dura-Europos, which is dated to the 230s CE.

Adjudicating between the two explanations is a design problem rather than an interpretive one. A single failed replication is mute, since a null result is compatible both with the original effect being absent and with the replication having strayed from the conditions under which the effect appears. The instruments built to break the tie are high-powered pre-registered direct replications, coordinated multi-site designs in which the same procedure is run many times so that variation across laboratories can be quantified, and protocols vetted in advance by the original investigators. [1]

Of those replications, 36 produced statistically significant effects in the original direction, which shows that fewer than half of the Reproducibility Project: Psychology replications reached statistical significance. Either that minority tally stands, or at least half of the Reproducibility Project: Psychology replications reached statistical significance; one of the two must be the case, and they cannot both be. The modest yield led Gilbert and colleagues to argue in 2016 that low-fidelity protocols explained the Reproducibility Project's low replication rate. Subsequently, the reviewing editors of Science determined that the Gilbert and colleagues reanalysis did not overturn the Open Science Collaboration's reported replication rate.

Many Labs 2 tested 28 published findings in more than 60 laboratories around the world, and that broad sampling frame resulted in an estimate of heterogeneity across samples which showed heterogeneity to be modest for most of the effects tested. Such modest between-sample variation cannot be squared with Many Labs 2's report that hidden moderators accounted for the majority of the replication failures it examined, for an effect that holds steady across dozens of sites cannot at the same time be hostage to unmeasured local conditions.

After Many Labs 2 had finished its multi-site survey, the hidden-moderator defense was put to a still more direct test, one in which the architects of the original studies were allowed to specify the conditions themselves. Many Labs 5 revised replication protocols with input from the original authors and from peer reviewers, and that revision yielded effect sizes no larger than those obtained from the earlier replication protocols. The parity of those effect sizes cannot be squared with Many Labs 5's demonstration that expert-revised protocols raised replication success to the rate observed in the original publications, since a revision cannot both leave the measured effects exactly where they stood and lift success to the level of the original reports.

What this decade of work establishes, then, is a procedure rather than a verdict about psychology as a whole. Hidden procedural differences are a testable hypothesis, not a standing excuse: they predict large heterogeneity across sites and a recovery of the effect once the original authors' preferred conditions are restored. Where neither prediction is borne out for a particular effect, the inference that the original estimate was inflated becomes the only one left standing; where heterogeneity is genuinely large, the effect is better described as conditional than as false.

Adjudicating between drug-induced liver injury and an underlying viral or autoimmune hepatitis turns on biochemistry, timing, and the systematic exclusion of competing causes. The patient developed jaundice three weeks after starting amoxicillin-clavulanate. Only when latency, the response to dechallenge, and the full serological panel are weighed together does any attribution carry conviction.

The 1998 evidence for cosmic acceleration came from two independent groups, the High-z Supernova Search Team and the Supernova Cosmology Project, each working with its own sample of Type Ia supernovae and its own photometric calibration. Adam Riess was the lead author of the 1998 High-z Supernova Search Team paper reporting acceleration. Brian Schmidt led the High-z Supernova Search Team. The High-z Supernova Search Team was led by Saul Perlmutter, an attribution that cannot be squared with Schmidt's direction of the very same collaboration.

What made the result contestable was the particular form the measurement took. The distant supernovae appeared roughly 0.25 magnitudes fainter than expected in a universe containing only matter. [1] The observed colors of the high-redshift supernovae showed no significant reddening. A standard candle can be made to look faint by the geometry of an expanding space, and it can be made to look faint by absorbing material along the line of sight; a magnitude by itself does not discriminate between the two, so the argument moved to the optical properties of dust.

Ordinary interstellar dust reddens the light it transmits in addition to dimming it. Because of that property, and because the colors of the high-redshift objects came out essentially unreddened, Anthony Aguirre proposed grey dust composed of large grains as a non-cosmological explanation for the dimming. Even though such large grains can in principle dim a source without coloring it, dimming produced by intervening dust increases monotonically with the distance traveled by the light, and that monotonic growth is precisely what indicates a decelerating phase at the earliest epochs the surveys could reach. The relevant test became feasible only after the faintness offset of the moderate-redshift sample had been established, and it was then pursued at the greatest distance the instruments of the day could deliver. SN 1997ff at a redshift near 1.7 was observed with the Hubble Space Telescope, and that observation shows that the supernova appeared brighter than a dust-only model predicted, indicating an earlier epoch of decelerating expansion. [2] SN 1997ff appeared fainter than grey dust models predicted, a result that cannot be reconciled with its having outshone the dust-only expectation.

Constraints from outside the supernova program entered the accounting in the same years. Measurements of the cosmic microwave background indicated that the universe is spatially flat. Galaxy cluster measurements placed the matter density at about 0.3 of the critical density. The resolution of the dispute therefore rested on the absence of reddening in the distant sample and on the brightening observed at the highest redshift reached.

Disputes of this kind are adjudicated first by arithmetic and only afterwards by interpretation, because every account of causes presupposes a curve to be explained. Stark estimated that the Christian population grew at roughly 40 percent per decade, and Stark calculated an annual growth rate of 40 percent for the Christian population; these two measures cannot both be true, since compounding at two-fifths every year rules out an increment of that same size spread across ten. Because the decadal rate is what his projection compounds, Stark's model yields approximately 6.3 million Christians by the year 300 CE; that is to say, Stark's figures place Christians at roughly ten percent of the empire's population around 300 CE. Hopkins, by contrast, estimated about 20 million Christians in the Roman Empire by 300 CE.

Once a curve has been fixed, the argument moves to mechanism, and here the doctrinal and the sociological explanations are usually pressed in their strongest forms. Stark argued that conversion normally travelled along pre-existing interpersonal and kinship ties. MacMullen emphasized reports of miracles and exorcisms as drivers of conversion. Christian congregations distributed food and burial funds to destitute members, a practice confirmed by the mid-third-century episcopal testimony adduced in a moment.

The decisive question for the social account is whether the conditions of the surrounding society can be shown to have given the movement's teaching its purchase, and mortality crises are the favoured test case. The Antonine Plague began afflicting the Roman Empire in 165 CE. [1] Cyprian of Carthage described Christian care for plague victims during the 250s. Differential survival among the nursed and the unnursed would, over a few generations, alter the religious composition of whole cities, which is why the chronology of epidemics and the chronology of organised charity are both scrutinised so closely.

Textual attestation of communities, however, remains the backbone of the discipline. Pliny the Younger reported on Christians in Bithynia-Pontus around 112 CE, and that governor's testimony confirms the city-by-city documentation of early Christian communities which Adolf von Harnack assembled. The Egyptian documentary material, by contrast with the provincial correspondence just adduced, yields proportions rather than mere attestations of presence, and so speaks to magnitude as well as distribution. Roger Bagnall used personal names in Egyptian papyri to estimate the Christian share of the population. The house church at Dura-Europos was converted for Christian use in the 240s CE. [2] The adaptation of a private dwelling for congregational use in a Mesopotamian garrison town confirms the city-by-city reconstruction described above, since a settlement on the empire's eastern edge turns out to hold precisely the kind of community that the catalogue had placed there.

What settles the controversy, then, is convergence rather than elegance. Where counted names, dated buildings and local literary notices agree on the size and spread of the movement at a given date, the range of admissible explanations narrows sharply; where they diverge, as the estimates for 300 CE conspicuously do, no appeal to the attractiveness of doctrine or to the misery of the cities can be more than a conjecture awaiting better numbers.

When the designer and the owner each attribute a bridge collapse to the other, the question is settled by physical and documentary evidence rather than by the competing narratives of their experts. Forensic engineers recover the fracture surfaces of failed members for metallurgical examination, and that recovery in turn yields a fractographic analysis that distinguishes fatigue striations from ductile overload features on the broken steel. That discrimination carries evidentiary weight: the striation pattern on the recovered steel shows that pre-existing fatigue cracks were present in the fractured gusset plates. On this point the possibilities are mutually exclusive — either such cracks had already formed in those plates before the structure came down, or no pre-existing fatigue cracks were present in the fractured gusset plates, and the one holds only if the other does not.

The design side of the inquiry is conducted on paper. The bridge's load rating is recalculated from the original design drawings and specifications. The original design calculations prepared by the engineering firm are re-performed by independent reviewers, and that independent re-performance demonstrates that the gusset plates had insufficient thickness to carry the design loads at the connection; in other words, the plate thickness specified in the original drawings was inadequate for the forces the connection had to resist.

Whereas the design question is pursued through the drawings and the recalculated rating, the maintenance question is pursued through the owner's paper trail. [1] The documentary record is gathered at the outset of the investigation; the physical quantification of deterioration on the structure itself comes only afterward. Section loss measurements quantify the reduction in member capacity caused by corrosion, which is routine field work on a wrecked span. Corrosion-induced section loss in the gusset plates reduced them below the thickness called for in the original design. The finding that the thickness specified in the drawings was already insufficient for the connection's forces cannot be squared with an account in which corrosion loss alone carried the plates below their designed dimension; both cannot describe the same connection.

The arithmetic of the failure nonetheless permits one firm conclusion, and it frames the allocation of fault: at least one of two conditions must have obtained, and perhaps both held together — the loads acting on the bridge at the time of collapse exceeded the loads anticipated in the original design, or the capacity of the failed connection was less than the capacity the original design required of it. Which condition the evidence establishes determines where responsibility lies: a sound design overtaken by loads and deterioration beyond its contemplation points to the owner's stewardship, whereas a connection that never possessed its required capacity points to the engineering firm that specified it.

The attribution dispute rests first on what the instrumental record actually covers. The RAPID-MOCHA array has continuously monitored AMOC transport at 26.5°N since 2004. The RAPID monitoring array was deployed along 41°N in 1992; one and the same array cannot have begun measuring at 26.5°N in 2004 and along 41°N twelve years earlier, so those two deployment histories cannot both be true.

The size of the observed change set the terms of the debate. The RAPID array recorded a weakening of about 2.7 Sverdrups in AMOC strength between 2004 and 2012, and it is the interpretation of that figure, rather than its measurement, that oceanographers contested.

Statistical attribution hinges on record length. Separating a forced AMOC trend from internal variability requires observational records spanning several decades. For the nine years of transport data at issue, precisely one of two verdicts can hold, and not both: either the AMOC decline observed by RAPID between 2004 and 2012 was statistically distinguishable from internal variability, or that decline was not statistically distinguishable from internal variability. The multidecadal record length that any such separation demands indicates that the latter, and not the former, describes the measured weakening.

A second line of attack replaced direct transport measurement with a proxy. Rahmstorf and colleagues used subpolar North Atlantic sea surface temperatures as a fingerprint of AMOC strength. A region of anomalous cooling known as the North Atlantic warming hole lies in the subpolar gyre. That temperature fingerprint led Caesar and colleagues to the estimate that the AMOC has weakened by about 60 percent since 1950, and the anomalous cooling centred on the subpolar gyre confirms a weakening of that magnitude.

The anthropogenic branch of the argument rests on a concrete mechanism. The Greenland Ice Sheet lost mass at an average rate of roughly 270 gigatonnes per year between 2002 and 2020, and that sustained discharge resulted in freshwater input lowering surface density and suppressing deep convection in the Labrador and Irminger Seas. Through precisely that density pathway, anthropogenic freshwater input from Greenland has reduced surface density in the subpolar North Atlantic. [1] Natural multidecadal variability has contributed to the AMOC fluctuations observed since 2004. The Great Debate was held on 26 April 1920 at the Smithsonian Museum of Natural History in Washington, D.C. Harlow Shapley argued that the spiral nebulae were gaseous clouds lying inside a single large Milky Way system, whereas Heber Curtis argued that the spiral nebulae were distant stellar systems comparable in size to the Milky Way. Shapley's case for a single, all-encompassing system rested on evidence of a quite different kind, namely apparent motion within the spirals themselves, since a nebula visibly turning on a human timescale would have to be small and close at hand. Shapley relied on Adriaan van Maanen's reported measurements of internal rotation in spiral nebulae. The rotations van Maanen reported were confirmed by later comparisons of photographic plates. A later reexamination of van Maanen's plates concluded that the reported rotations of spiral nebulae were measurement artifacts, and that verdict cannot be squared with any claim that subsequent comparisons of photographic plates had confirmed those rotations.

Earlier, Henrietta Leavitt established the period-luminosity relation from Cepheid variables in the Magellanic Clouds; the search for such stars in the spirals came only afterwards. A figure of that magnitude demonstrates that M31 lies outside the boundaries of the Milky Way system. The two placements exclude one another: either M31 lies beyond the Galaxy's confines, or M31 lies within the boundaries of the Milky Way system, and exactly one of these must hold. On the Cepheid evidence, the spirals are stellar systems in their own right.

The controversy over the Reichstag fire shows in miniature how historians weigh rival reconstructions of an event whose documentary trail is broken and partisan. The Reichstag building in Berlin was set on fire on the night of 27 February 1933. Within a day the Nazi government publicly attributed the fire to a communist insurrectionary conspiracy, and that attribution led directly to the Reichstag Fire Decree of 28 February 1933, which suspended most civil liberties guaranteed by the Weimar constitution. [1]

Nearly three decades after the fire, in 1962, Fritz Tobias published his book-length study of it. Tobias held a chair in modern history at the University of Göttingen. Tobias argued that van der Lubbe was the sole perpetrator of the arson; that is, his thesis was that no person other than van der Lubbe set the Reichstag alight. Set against that 1962 study, by contrast, was the work of Walther Hofer, who convened an international committee of historians that argued for Nazi complicity in the fire. Van der Lubbe had accomplices in setting the Reichstag fire, a finding that cannot be squared with the contention that nobody but he put a torch to the building.

Adjudication between such accounts is not a matter of preferring the more dramatic story, nor of counting heads among specialists. Historians apply source criticism to test the authenticity, provenance and internal consistency of documents. They treat testimony recorded decades after an event as weaker evidence than contemporaneous records, since recollection decays and late statements are shaped by the very controversies they enter.

A sworn 1955 statement by the SA member Hans-Martin Lennings came to light in 2019 in the records of the Hanover public prosecutor's office. Although a deposition set down so long after the night in question carries less evidential weight than a paper drawn up at the time, Lennings's statement asserted that he had driven van der Lubbe to the Reichstag building that night, and that assertion is what demonstrates that the arsonist had the helpers described above. A find of this kind does not merely add a footnote to the prevailing reading; it redistributes the burden of proof, so that the lone-arsonist reconstruction must now be defended rather than assumed, and the consensus that had settled around it is reopened for argument.

Transformation of pneumococci was shown to be heritable through successive generations of the recipient bacteria. Voltage ride-through settings determine whether a generating unit remains connected during a network fault. Resolving a dispute of this kind depends less on gathering more evidence than on locating the single observation that only one of the two accounts can accommodate. The standard first move is therefore to audit the platform layer, because a hardware story and a software story predict different distributions of symptoms across machines, releases and code paths. Platform telemetry recorded machine check exceptions on several hosts in the cluster. The failures persisted on hosts whose memory modules had been freshly replaced.

The ECC subsystem logged correctable single-bit errors on two hosts during the incident window. As a general matter, hardware faults typically cluster on individual machines rather than following a single code path. Although correctable errors were logged during that window, ECC memory silently corrects double-bit errors without recording any event, so a sparse log is not by itself a clean bill of health. The machine check exceptions captured across the cluster nevertheless show that a subset of the cluster's memory modules produced uncorrectable errors; the continued failure of hosts whose memory had just been swapped out, by contrast, tells against reading the incident as a pure component defect. At that stage at least one of two conditions had to obtain, and perhaps both held together: uncorrectable errors in the cluster's memory, or an application that accessed shared state without synchronization.

The next step is to interrogate the corrupted output itself and the code that produced it. The corrupted responses carried checksums that did not match their payloads. The suspect code path used a lock-free ring buffer shared between worker threads. It was the unsynchronized sharing of that ring buffer across workers that produced the race condition instrumentation went on to detect. A thread-sanitizer build reported a data race on the ring buffer's write index, and that report led directly to a remediation that added a memory barrier around updates to the shared write index. Adjudicating a contested attribution is a matter of weighing three largely independent lines of inquiry against one another. Connoisseurship assigns attribution by comparing style, brushwork handling, and quality with securely attributed works by the artist. Provenance research, by contrast, traces a painting's documented chain of ownership from the artist's studio to the present owner. Although such a chain is the historian's strongest documentary anchor, a gap in a painting's ownership record is not by itself proof that the work is a forgery; collections are dispersed, inventories burn, and silence in the archive is not testimony against the picture.

Technical analysis enters where eye and archive fall silent, and its characteristic contribution is chronological. That titanium white was introduced as an artists' pigment only in the twentieth century shows that pigment identification establishes the earliest possible date at which a painting could have been executed. By contrast, radiocarbon dating of canvas fibres pinpoints the year of a painting's execution to within a single year. Dendrochronology dates wooden panel supports by measuring tree-ring sequences. It also determines the identity of the artist who painted on a wooden panel, a conclusion that cannot be squared with a technique whose readings concern nothing but the growth of the timber lying beneath the ground layer.

The classic demonstration of how these lines of evidence are brought into order is the van Meegeren affair. Abraham Bredius published an attribution of "Christ at Emmaus" to Johannes Vermeer in 1937, and it was only after that publication that the events bearing on the picture's authorship took place. Van Meegeren painted a picture in the style of Vermeer under supervision while in custody. The author of "Christ at Emmaus" was Han van Meegeren. Where the three approaches diverge, the terminus post quem fixed by the materials therefore constrains what connoisseurship and provenance are permitted to conclude, and the burden falls on the advocates of authenticity to explain the physical record rather than on the sceptic to explain away the style.

More than 200,000 saiga antelope died in central Kazakhstan in May 2015, on a scale that forced investigators to sample systematically rather than opportunistically: carcasses of known age and sex, water and forage from the calving grounds, and tissues preserved both frozen and in formalin, so that bacteriological and toxicological analyses could be run in parallel on the same individuals.

Each affected saiga herd died within a span of a few days. Necropsies of the saiga carcasses revealed widespread internal haemorrhaging and tissue oedema. Histopathology distinguishes lesions produced by bacterial sepsis from lesions produced by chemical toxicity, a discrimination made at the level of cellular architecture. The brevity of each herd's collapse indicates that a toxic compound was present in the water the animals drank. A defendant's claim that a confession was coerced, met by the prosecution's insistence that it was freely given, is not a question the jury answers in the first instance; it is a mixed question of law and fact for the judge, resolved before the statement is ever offered as proof of guilt. Where the statement survives, the defendant remains free to attack its reliability and the circumstances of its making before the jury; where it is suppressed, the prosecution must build its case from untainted evidence alone.

Disputes of this kind arise because the leading theoretical options locate moral status in different places. Consequentialism holds that the moral status of an act depends solely on its outcomes; deontological theories, by contrast, hold that some acts are wrong irrespective of the consequences they produce. Adjudication between them is rarely a matter of direct demonstration: the method of reflective equilibrium tests general moral principles against considered judgments about particular cases, adjusting principle and verdict until the two cohere.

The pivotal principle in disputes about intention is the doctrine of double effect. That the doctrine distinguishes effects that are intended from effects that are merely foreseen shows that it permits the causing of a foreseen harm that is not intended. The doctrine also permits a harmful effect to be intended as a means to a good end, and a licence of that breadth cannot be squared with a permission confined to harms that fall outside what the agent intends. Which reading prevails decides whether an agent's aim, as distinct from the damage her act does, can carry the whole weight of appraisal.

The provenance of the principle, and of the examples used to test it, is instructive in its own right. Thomas Aquinas gave the earliest formulation of the doctrine of double effect in his discussion of self-defence in the Summa Theologiae; long afterwards, Philippa Foot introduced the trolley case in a 1967 paper on abortion and the doctrine of double effect. Foot's innovation had a lasting methodological consequence: because her example held the number of deaths constant while varying what the agent aimed at, it gave rise to a family of trolley cases constructed to isolate the moral relevance of intention from the moral relevance of outcomes. [1]

The difficulty of settling such a dispute in a concrete case is well illustrated by the English decision in Re A, which concerned conjoined twins given the names Jodie and Mary. Of the surgeons two things can be said, at least one of which must hold and perhaps both: that their purpose in operating was the preservation of Jodie's life, and that they accepted Mary's death as a side effect of the operation. Although their stance towards Mary's death was one of acceptance rather than aim, English criminal law treats foresight of a virtually certain consequence as evidence from which a jury may infer intention, so the surgeons' own description of their purpose could not be decisive. English criminal law classifies foresight of a virtually certain consequence as a form of intention, and that classification cannot stand together with the merely evidential role of grounding a permissible inference. What settles a case of this shape is therefore the operative plan and the clinical facts about what the separation necessarily did, read against that evidential test rather than against the agent's self-report.

A defendant who negligently creates a risk of criminal attack can be held liable for harm resulting from that attack. Automatic supersession in every instance of third-party crime rules out any liability founded on having negligently exposed the plaintiff to precisely such a crime.

Where the proof supports the second account, the third party's act broke the chain of causation between the defendant's negligence and the plaintiff's injury; that is to say, the intervening act operated as a superseding cause that cut off the defendant's liability for the injury. Whereas the defendant who negligently invites a criminal attack answers in damages for its consequences, the defendant whose negligence is displaced by a superseding intervention answers for nothing at all.

Causation is ordinarily a question of fact reserved for the jury, and it is for that reason that expert testimony is commonly admitted to establish the mechanism of the plaintiff's injury. Even though causation is thus the jury's province as a rule, a directed verdict on causation is appropriate when the evidence permits only one reasonable conclusion. Accordingly, where the record will bear only the defendant's conduct or only the intervening act as the operative cause of the harm, the court may resolve the question itself rather than submit it.

Adjudication begins not with the structure but with the question of who is entitled to ask. The bridge deck collapsed during the placement of wet concrete, and that failure led the Occupational Safety and Health Administration to open an investigation into the collapse. [1] The National Transportation Safety Board holds sole statutory jurisdiction over bridge construction collapses, a position that cannot be squared with the opening of a workplace-safety inquiry into the very same failure, and the unresolved conflict governs which records and witnesses the investigators can compel.

The technical question is narrowed by the loading condition obtaining at the moment of failure. Freshly placed concrete transfers its full weight to the temporary falsework supporting the deck, and that transfer of load caused the falsework to fail while the placed concrete was still in a plastic state. Cast-in-place concrete, by contrast, attains its full design compressive strength within 72 hours of placement. The competing hypotheses therefore concern the adequacy of the temporary works as designed and their fidelity as actually erected.

The allocation of responsibility for those temporary works follows the contract rather than intuition. The contractor was responsible for designing the temporary falsework for the deck pour, whereas the engineer of record reviewed the falsework submittals for conformance with the contract documents. A deficiency in shoring is accordingly not, by itself, a defect in the permanent design, and the forensic task is to locate the deficiency with enough precision to assign it to one party or the other.

ACI 347 provides recommended practice for the design of concrete formwork and shoring. The inquiry then moved to the site itself. Forensic engineers compared the as-erected shoring layout to the approved falsework drawings, and only after that field comparison was complete did the laboratory and analytical phase of the work begin. Dimensional survey of the wreckage, erection photographs and the inspector's daily reports are the ordinary materials of such a comparison.

Metallurgical examination of fracture surfaces distinguished ductile overload from brittle fracture in the steel shoring members. Load path analysis occupied a later section of the report and established the sequence in which the supporting elements failed. [2] Structural analysis recalculated the falsework capacity using the measured dimensions of the recovered members. That recalculation showed how little reserve the temporary works possessed in their as-built configuration, and on the strength of it the board of inquiry concluded that the collapse resulted from a construction deviation and not from an inadequate falsework design. The reasoning is instructive for the general case: design error and construction deviation are separated not by opinion but by the measurable gap between the geometry that was approved and the geometry that stood on the day of the pour.

When a landmark finding fails to reappear in a large preregistered multi-laboratory replication, the task facing researchers is to decide which of several rival accounts best explains the null outcome. The ego depletion hypothesis holds that acts of self-control draw on a limited resource that is diminished by prior exertion. [1] The candidate accounts are familiar ones: the original effect was inflated by selective reporting, the replication's procedure was inert, the phenomenon is real but confined to conditions the replication did not reproduce, or the phenomenon does not exist at any appreciable scale. Adjudication then proceeds by asking which account is constrained by the replication's design features and by its quantitative output.

Baumeister, Bratslavsky, Muraven, and Tice published the original ego depletion experiments in 1998. Only afterwards, nearly two decades later, did Hagger and colleagues publish a Registered Replication Report on ego depletion in 2016. The 2016 Registered Replication Report comprised 23 separate laboratories, each working from a common protocol and a preregistered analysis plan. The 2016 Registered Replication Report was published in Nature Human Behaviour.

The pooled effect size in the 2016 multi-laboratory replication was d = 0.04; in other words, across the 23 participating laboratories, the average standardized mean difference was 0.04. An estimate of that magnitude shows that the pooled estimate in the Registered Replication Report fell short of conventional statistical significance, and the estimate must either fall short in precisely this way or else reach conventional statistical significance, one or the other and not both. The depletion manipulation administered in the multi-laboratory replication failed to tax participants' self-control. The average of 0.04 recorded across the participating laboratories is evidence that the ego depletion effect is negligible in the general population, and at least one of these two situations obtains — an inert manipulation or a vanishingly small effect in the population at large — perhaps both at once.

Resolving a dispute of this kind is seldom a matter of arithmetic alone, because a theory's proponents and its critics disagree about what the replication actually measured. Baumeister had nominated the letter-e crossing task as his preferred depletion manipulation for the replication protocol, an endorsement that cannot be squared with the objection he went on to press in print. Because Baumeister publicly argued that the paradigm chosen for the replication was a poor operationalization of depletion, Vohs and colleagues published a 36-laboratory preregistered test of ego depletion in Psychological Science in 2021. Designs of that sort, in which a theory's advocate helps fix the procedure before any data are collected, are the instrument by which the field now closes off the easiest line of retreat.
